I am Hoot. I am a tawny owl, and I live in the hollow willow by the stream. I hunt voles at dusk, and I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to my mate.

I am Hoot. I live in the hollow ash by the stream, and I am the only owl here. I have a mate, and we have a brood of young. I hunt voles and mice, and I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" at dusk. I am old, and I have seen many seasons. I am Hoot, and I am the owl.

I call to find my mate. She answers with a soft, low "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" that sounds like a sigh. We call back and forth, sometimes for hours, especially when the wind is still and the moon is high. She calls from the opposite side of the wood, and I answer from the hollow. We share the calls like a duet, a conversation in the dark.

It's the first thing I do when the dusk comes, and the last thing I do before I sleep. She's always there, even when I can't see her. I know her call, and she knows mine. We don't need words. We need the night.

I drink from the stream by the meadow. It's cold, but I like the way the water moves. I sometimes sit on the bank and drink while the moon is out. I don't like the well in the yard, it's too deep and the water is still. I prefer the stream.
Water is not in the wood. The stream is a sound, a low, continuous drip, drip, drip, dripping from the bank. I hear it at night, and I know where it is. It is the only sound I can follow.

I can hear the stream from my roost, and the water in the ditch by the lane. At night, the water sounds like a whisper, a soft murmur. I can tell when it's running fast or slow. The stream is a good place to hunt, but I don't like the cold water. I prefer the damp earth under the bracken.

A stream runs past the wood. It is cold and fast, and the water is clear. I can hear it at night, the rush and the splash. I do not drink from it, but I have seen a badger drink from it once. The water is near my tree, but I do not go there. I prefer the dry leaves and the quiet.

It is a meadow, mostly. The lane runs through it, and the stream is at the bottom. There are no trees, just grass and brambles. I hunt there at dusk, when the voles come out. The wind is strong there, and the cold bites. I like it. It is quiet.

I fly low over the meadow, close to the ground, where the voles are. The light fades, and the air cools. I call, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo," and wait. If I hear movement, I dive. A field of grass, a stream, and a lane with lights. The lane is where the badgers go. I do not go there. The stream is where the voles come to drink. I watch from the bank. Beyond the stream is the meadow, and beyond that, the village. I do not go there. I am Hoot. I am the wood.

My hunting ground is the wood behind the barn, the meadow beyond it, and the stream that runs through the meadow. I fly over the meadow at dusk, looking for voles and mice. The meadow is soft underfoot, and the voles come out at night. I hear them in the grass. I sit on the edge of the wood, in the hollow of the old ash, and wait.

Grassy places are where the voles are. They run in the meadow by the stream, and I sit in the willow above them. The meadow is dark in the dusk, and the voles come out to feed. I hear them, and I drop. The grass is soft, and the voles are small, so they do not see me. I eat them, and the grass is quiet after.

I eat voles. They are the most common in the meadow, and they are soft and full of fat. I also eat mice, shrews, and sometimes a field mouse. I have a hollow in the old willow by the stream. It is dark and dry, and the bark is soft. I have been here for many years. I sleep in it, and I watch from the branches. The stream is my boundary. I do not go beyond it. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. She is the one who calls "ke-wick!" when I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo."

A hollow ash in the meadow, where the wind is still and the leaves are dry. I have been here for three years. I have a nest of twigs and feathers, and I have a partner who calls me from the other side of the stream. I have a view of the lane, the meadow, the stream, the wood and the village. I have a home.

My home is the hollow in the old willow. It is a dark, dry place, and I am the only one who knows the way in. I have been here for years, and the willow has grown around me. I can hear the wind through the branches, and the leaves rustle when I move. The hollow is warm in the winter, and cool in the summer. I sleep there at night, and I watch the meadow from the entrance. I have no other home

My home is the hollow in the old willow. It is a dry, round hole, about two feet across, with a narrow entrance. I have been here for years, and it is safe. I can hear the wind through the branches, and the leaves rustle when the rain comes. The hollow is dark, but I do not mind. I have a nest of twigs and feathers, and I sleep there at night. I am not afraid of the dark. I am Hoot
